1.title: Context, Tokens and Prompt Reuse
1.text: Welcome to Module six: Context, Tokens and Prompt Reuse. This module covers context, tokens and prompt reuse. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. The context window as a budget and how to stay inside it. Context engineering techniques: pruning, compaction, isolation, external memory. Prompt caching: rules, ordering and savings. Modular prompts and Skills (progressive disclosure). Token optimization levers and measurement.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory and the Retail Client's Slow, Costly Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory and the Retail Client's Slow, Costly Assistant. A retailer's assistant sends a twelve thousand-token policy and catalog extract on every request, plus the full chat history. By the afternoon, answers drift and the bill is three times the forecast.

1.title: The Context Is a Budget
1.text: The Context Is a Budget. Everything in the window competes: system prompt, tools, history, documents, tool results. More is not better; relevant and well ordered is better. The A P I (application programming interface) is stateless: you resend what the model needs. Tokens are billed as input and output; thinking tokens bill as output. Context drift and bloat raise cost and latency and lower quality. Use token counting (an estimate endpoint) to plan prompts, route models and fit budgets.

1.title: The Context Is a Budget, continued
1.text: The Context Is a Budget, continued. The figure shows this: The context window is a budget: stable prefix, tools, history, retrieved passages and tool results compete; prune, compact, isolate and store outside to stay within it.

1.title: The Context Is a Budget, continued
1.text: The Context Is a Budget, continued. Prune tool output. What it does: Keep only fields the next step needs. Use when: Tools return verbose records. Compaction. What it does: Replace older turns with a summary (server-side or your own call). Use when: Long conversations near the limit. Context editing. What it does: Clear old tool results automatically. Use when: Agent loops with big results. Isolation. What it does: Do verbose work in a subagent; return a summary. Use when: Exploration would flood the main window. External memory. What it does: Store facts in files or a store; load when relevant (memory tool). Use when: Facts must outlive the window. Just-in-time retrieval. What it does: Fetch documents when needed. Use when: Large corpora (Module nine).

1.title: The Context Is a Budget, continued
1.text: The Context Is a Budget, continued. Ordering. What it does: Long documents first; question and instructions last. Use when: Long-context prompts. Compaction can lose exact figures and commitments: keep them in a persistent block resent each turn. A one million token window does not remove the need for retrieval on very large corpora, and long contexts cost more and can dilute attention.

1.title: Prompt Caching
1.text: Prompt Caching. The figure shows this: Prompt caching: the stable prefix before the breakpoint is written once and read on later requests; only the changing suffix is processed fresh.

1.title: Prompt Caching, continued
1.text: Prompt Caching, continued. Prefix order. Tools, then system, then messages; the cache covers the exact prefix up to a breakpoint. Breakpoints. Automatic caching with one top-level cache control, or explicit breakpoints (at most four). T T L. five minutes (default) or one hour; refreshed when the entry is read. Minimum. About five hundred twelve tokens on current tiers; shorter prompts run without caching and without an error. Price. Reads are a fraction of base input (ten percent; five percent or two point five percent on some tiers); writes one point two five times (five min) or two times (one hour).

1.title: Prompt Caching, continued
1.text: Prompt Caching, continued. Invalidation. Any change in the prefix (a timestamp, a reordered tool, a different tool set) breaks the match. Check. usage fields cache creation input tokens and cache read input tokens. Stable content first, dynamic last. Never put timestamps, user names or random I Ds before the cached text. Keep tool definitions stable (deferred tool loading preserves the prefix; Module seven). Caching reduces latency and cost together; it helps only when the same prefix repeats within the T T L. It also makes contextual retrieval and large few-shot blocks cheap to reuse (Module nine). Exam tip: For a long, repeated static prompt with a short varying question, the best single optimization is caching the stable prefix (static first). Truncating needed context or shrinking the model blindly are the distractors.

1.title: Modular Prompts and Skills
1.text: Modular Prompts and Skills. Modular prompts: compose a prompt from versioned blocks (safety, tone, task, schema, tool guidance). Shared blocks keep many assistants consistent. Skills package procedures, scripts and reference files that Claude loads only when relevant. Metadata (name, description). Loaded: Always, in the system prompt. Cost: Small. Skill dot M D instructions. Loaded: When the skill triggers. Cost: Moderate. Resources and scripts. Loaded: As needed; scripts run without their code entering the context. Cost: Only when used.

1.title: Modular Prompts and Skills, continued
1.text: Modular Prompts and Skills, continued. The figure shows this: Skills use progressive disclosure: metadata always, instructions when triggered, resources and scripts on demand. Use a Skill for a repeatable procedure (report format, review checklist); use a Project or knowledge store for background; use M C P (Model Context Protocol) for live data and actions. Write precise descriptions (they decide when a skill triggers).

1.title: Token Optimization Levers
1.text: Token Optimization Levers. Cache the prefix. Cuts input cost and time-to-first-token on repeats. Shorter prompts and examples. Fewer input tokens. Ask for concise output; set max tokens. Fewer output tokens (blunt cap cuts mid-sentence). Structured output. Short, parseable answers. Route to smaller tiers. Lower price per token. Batch A P I. fifty percent off for non-urgent work. Prune, compact, isolate. Smaller context per turn. Lower effort. Fewer thinking tokens. Measure first (token counts, cache hit rate, cost per request) before optimizing (Module twelve). Exam tip: Any change before the cache breakpoint (a timestamp, a reordered tool) breaks the cache; put variable text after the stable prefix. Exam tip: Compaction can lose exact figures: keep numbers and commitments in a persistent block.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Context: A budget; stateless A P I; thinking bills as output. Techniques: Prune, compact, edit, isolate, external memory, just-in-time retrieval. Cache: Static first; prefix exact; max four breakpoints; five min or one hour; about five hundred twelve minimum. Savings: Reads ten percent (five percent or two point five percent some tiers); writes one point two five times or two times. Break: Any change in the prefix. Skills: Metadata always; instructions on trigger; resources on demand. Tokens: Cache, trim, concise output, route, batch, lower effort; measure first.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. An assistant resends a twelve thousand-token catalog extract with every request, followed by a short user message. Which change cuts cost and latency most directly? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A repeated stable prefix is what caching reuses.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Cache hits stopped after a developer added the current time to the start of the system prompt. Why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Any change in the prefix breaks the cache; put variable text after it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A conversation nears the context limit and must keep exact contract numbers. What is the best approach? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Summaries can lose exact values; protect them separately.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Select two. Which two describe how Skills reduce context cost? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Progressive disclosure keeps most content out of the window until needed.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A prompt of three hundred tokens is sent with cache control. No caching occurs and no error is returned. What is the likely reason? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Prompts under the minimum run uncached without an error; check the usage fields.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which action is most likely to improve both latency and cost for repetitive long prompts? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Reuse of the static prefix reduces processing time and price.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A subagent explores two hundred files to answer a question. How should its results reach the lead agent? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Returning a concise summary keeps the subagent's raw exploration out of the lead's window and the lead's context small.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: B. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: A and E. Question five: D. Question six: C. Question seven: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
